questions.question: On centimetre grid paper, Rectangle A is 2 squares wide and 6 squares tall. Rectangle B is 3 squares wide and 5 squares tall. Every small square is 1 cm by 1 cm, so Rectangle A covers 12 squares and Rectangle B covers 15 squares. Which sentence about these two rectangles is true?
options: They have the same perimeter (16 cm each) but different areas: 12 squares and 15 squares.
Their perimeters are equal, so their areas must be equal too.
They have the same area (16 squares each) but different perimeters.
Rectangle B has the longer perimeter because it covers more squares.
questions.explain: Count around the outside for perimeter (2+6+2+6 = 16 cm and 3+5+3+5 = 16 cm) and count the squares inside for area (12 and 15). The usual trap is thinking equal perimeters force equal areas — the same border can wrap different amounts of space.

questions.question: Two shapes are built from 12 identical 1 cm by 1 cm grid squares with no gaps. Shape A is 3 rows of 4 squares. Shape B is 1 row of 12 squares. Which sentence is true?
options: Both shapes have the same perimeter because both cover 12 squares.
Both shapes cover 12 square centimetres, but Shape B has the longer perimeter (26 cm compared with 14 cm).
Shape A has an area of 14 square centimetres and Shape B has an area of 26 square centimetres.
Shape B has the bigger area because its perimeter is longer.
questions.explain: Both shapes are made of 12 squares, so both areas are 12 square centimetres; walk the outside edge to get the perimeters, 4+3+4+3 = 14 cm and 12+1+12+1 = 26 cm. The trap is reading 14 and 26 as areas — those numbers count edge units, not squares.

questions.question: On centimetre grid paper Nadia draws a rectangle that is 5 squares long and 3 squares wide, so it covers 15 squares and its perimeter is 16 cm. Which rectangle below has the SAME perimeter as Nadia's but a DIFFERENT area?
options: A rectangle 15 squares long and 1 square wide
A rectangle 8 squares long and 2 squares wide
A rectangle 7 squares long and 1 square wide
A rectangle 3 squares long and 5 squares wide
questions.explain: For a perimeter of 16 cm the two side lengths must add to 8, so 7 and 1 works and gives an area of only 7 squares instead of 15. The 15-by-1 choice keeps the area the same but changes the perimeter to 32 cm — that is the opposite of what was asked.

questions.question: All the rectangles below are drawn on centimetre grid paper, where each square is 1 cm by 1 cm. Which PAIR has the same area but different perimeters?
options: A 2-by-6 rectangle and a 3-by-5 rectangle
A 4-by-5 rectangle and another 4-by-5 rectangle
A 3-by-4 rectangle and a 6-by-8 rectangle
A 2-by-9 rectangle and a 3-by-6 rectangle
questions.explain: Multiply for area and add all four sides for perimeter: 2 x 9 and 3 x 6 both cover 18 squares, yet the perimeters are 22 cm and 18 cm. The 2-by-6 and 3-by-5 pair is the reverse situation (same 16 cm perimeter, areas 12 and 15), so it answers a different question.

questions.question: A rectangular garden bed at a Kelowna school will be edged with exactly 20 m of cedar board, and the side lengths must be whole metres. Which shape gives the gardeners the GREATEST planting area?
options: 5 m by 5 m
8 m by 2 m
6 m by 4 m
9 m by 1 m
questions.explain: Every choice uses 20 m of edging, so compare areas with length x width: 9, 16, 24 and 25 square metres. The trap is assuming a fixed perimeter fixes the area — the closer a rectangle is to a square, the more space it encloses.

questions.question: Rectangle A measures 6 cm by 6 cm. Rectangle B measures 12 cm by 3 cm. Both have an area of 36 square centimetres. Which statement compares them correctly?
options: Their areas are equal, so their perimeters are equal too — both are 24 cm.
Their areas are equal, but B has a perimeter of 30 cm, which is 6 cm longer than A's 24 cm.
Rectangle B has the larger area because it has the larger perimeter.
Both have a perimeter of 36 cm, because their area is 36 square centimetres.
questions.explain: Add all four sides for each: 6+6+6+6 = 24 cm and 12+3+12+3 = 30 cm, even though both cover 36 square centimetres. Stretching a shape thinner keeps the area the same while the border gets longer, so never copy the area number into the perimeter.

questions.question: Liam wants to prove to his group that two rectangles can have the SAME AREA but DIFFERENT PERIMETERS. Which pair should he measure and show them?
options: 2 cm by 3 cm and 4 cm by 6 cm
2 cm by 10 cm and 4 cm by 8 cm
2 cm by 10 cm and 4 cm by 5 cm
3 cm by 6 cm and 6 cm by 3 cm
questions.explain: Check areas first: 2 x 10 and 4 x 5 both give 20 square centimetres, while the perimeters are 24 cm and 18 cm — exactly the point he wants to make. The 2-by-10 and 4-by-8 pair shares a 24 cm perimeter with different areas, which proves the opposite statement.

questions.question: A rectangle measures 8 cm by 3 cm. A second rectangle has the SAME perimeter, whole-centimetre sides, and the greatest area possible. What is the area of the second rectangle?
options: 24 square centimetres
10 square centimetres
22 square centimetres
30 square centimetres
questions.explain: The perimeter is 8+3+8+3 = 22 cm, so the length and width must add to 11; the most square-like pair, 6 and 5, gives 30 square centimetres. Answering 24 assumes the same perimeter must give the same area, and 22 copies the perimeter number into the area.

questions.question: Each student in a Victoria school garden club gets 26 m of wooden edging to build one rectangular plot. Ava builds a plot 10 m by 3 m. Noah builds a plot 8 m by 5 m. Both used all 26 m of edging. Who has more soil to plant in, and why?
options: Noah's, because with the same perimeter the squarer 8 m by 5 m plot covers 40 square metres while 10 m by 3 m covers only 30.
Ava's, because her plot has the longer side, and a 10 m side stretches out more growing space than an 8 m side ever could.
Both plots hold 26 square metres of soil, because each used 26 m of edging, and the edging length is also the growing space.
Neither — using the same 26 m of edging means the same growing space, since equal borders always enclose equal areas.
questions.explain: Both plots have a perimeter of 26 m, so compare growing space with length x width: 10 x 3 = 30 and 8 x 5 = 40 square metres. Equal edging does not mean equal soil — the squarer a rectangle is, the more area the same border encloses.

questions.question: A Burnaby community garden gives every family a plot with an area of 24 square metres. The Chen family's plot is 4 m by 6 m and the Singh family's plot is 2 m by 12 m. Each family fences all four sides of their own plot, and fencing costs $9 per metre. How much MORE does the Singh family pay for fencing?
options: $0, because the plots have the same area, so the fences cost the same
questions.explain: Fencing follows the perimeter: 4+6+4+6 = 20 m costs $180, and 2+12+2+12 = 28 m costs $252, a difference of $72. Same area does not mean same perimeter, and the 24 square metres must not be multiplied by the per-metre fence price.

questions.question: Jayden says, 'My rectangular hockey poster has a bigger perimeter than Mia's, so it must have a bigger area.' Which pair of poster sizes shows that Jayden's rule is WRONG?
options: Jayden's poster is 6 cm by 8 cm and Mia's is 3 cm by 4 cm.
Jayden's perimeter is 22 cm and Mia's is 18 cm, so Jayden's area is 22 square centimetres and Mia's is 18 square centimetres.
Jayden's poster is 1 cm by 10 cm and Mia's is 4 cm by 5 cm.
Jayden's poster is 3 cm by 7 cm and Mia's is 2 cm by 5 cm.
questions.explain: To disprove the rule you need a bigger perimeter with a smaller area: 1 by 10 has perimeter 22 cm but area 10 square centimetres, while 4 by 5 has perimeter 18 cm and area 20 square centimetres. Pairs where both numbers grow together only agree with Jayden, so they prove nothing.

questions.question: A Kamloops school has 30 m of wooden edging for one rectangular sandbox and will use all of it. Design A is 12 m by 3 m and Design B is 9 m by 6 m. Sand to fill the sandbox costs $5 per square metre. How much MORE will the sand for Design B cost than the sand for Design A?
options: $0, because both designs use 30 m of edging, so they hold the same sand
questions.explain: Both designs have a 30 m perimeter, so find each area: 12 x 3 = 36 and 9 x 6 = 54 square metres, a difference of 18 square metres, and 18 x $5 = $90. Sand fills area, not perimeter, so the 30 m must never be multiplied by the price.
